ra: Augustine of Hippo is one of the four traditional Latin Doctors and a paradigmatic Church Father.
Jerome is one of the four traditional Latin Doctors of the Church.
Ambrose of Milan is one of the four traditional Latin Doctors of the Church.
Gregory the Great is the last of the four traditional Latin Doctors of the Church.
Origen is a foundational early patristic theologian, conventionally grouped among the Church Fathers.
Irenaeus of Lyons is a major 2nd-century Church Father.
Tertullian is the first major Latin Father, conventionally grouped among the Church Fathers.
Cyprian of Carthage is a 3rd-century Latin Church Father.
Justin Martyr is the foremost 2nd-century Greek apologist, counted among the Church Fathers.
Clement of Alexandria is an early Alexandrian Church Father.
Clement of Rome is one of the Apostolic Fathers, the earliest stratum of the Church Fathers.
Ignatius of Antioch is one of the Apostolic Fathers.
Polycarp of Smyrna is one of the Apostolic Fathers.
Hilary of Poitiers is a Latin Doctor and Church Father.
Leo the Great is a Doctor of the Church and a patristic Father.
John of Damascus is traditionally counted as the last of the Greek Church Fathers.
Bede is a Doctor of the Church often grouped with the late Latin Fathers.
Isidore of Seville is a Doctor of the Church, frequently called the last of the Latin Fathers.
Gregory of Nyssa is one of the three Cappadocian Fathers.
Cyril of Alexandria is a Doctor of the Church and Greek Father.
Maximus the Confessor is a foundational late Greek/Byzantine Father.

Augustine was catechized and baptized by Ambrose of Milan, whose preaching he credits in the Confessions with his conversion.
Origen is traditionally held to have studied under Clement of Alexandria at the Alexandrian catechetical school (succession reported by Eusebius).
Irenaeus reports in his letter to Florinus that he heard Polycarp of Smyrna in his youth, linking him to the apostolic generation.
Gregory of Nyssa was the younger brother of Basil the Great; both were Cappadocian Fathers.
Gregory of Nyssa, Basil, and Gregory the Theologian (Nazianzen) form the three Cappadocian Fathers who jointly developed pro-Nicene Trinitarian theology.
Hilary of Poitiers was called 'the Athanasius of the West' for leading the Latin defense of Nicene orthodoxy against Arianism, paralleling Athanasius in the East.
Gregory the Great's pastoral and grace theology drew on, and transmitted to the medieval West, the doctrine of Augustine of Hippo.
John of Damascus's dogmatic synthesis (the Fount of Knowledge) systematized earlier Greek patristic theology, notably the Christology of Maximus the Confessor.
Cyril of Alexandria self-consciously continued the Alexandrian Christological and anti-heretical tradition of his predecessor in the see, Athanasius.
Bede's Ecclesiastical History venerates and depends on Gregory the Great, who initiated the Gregorian mission that converted Bede's English church.
Isidore of Seville's encyclopedic and theological works compile and transmit the Latin patristic heritage, especially Augustine.
Augustine, a former Manichaean auditor, became a leading opponent of Manichaeism, attacking Mani's system in Contra Faustum and other works. Object verified as ENT_MANICH_MANI.
Beyond baptism, Augustine's exegetical method and Trinitarian thought were decisively shaped by Ambrose's allegorical preaching, as he records in the Confessions.
